title: How do OAuth2/OIDC work in Spring Security? What is the declarative HTTP client (@HttpExchange)? What is WebFlux (Mono/Flux)? How do WebSocket/SSE work? What is GraphQL in Spring? What is Spring AI? How does Quarkus differ from Spring Boot?
shortTitle: What is OAuth2 Resource Server and WebFlux?
keyPoints: An OAuth2 Resource Server does not issue tokens -- it validates incoming JWTs by fetching the issuer's public key (JWKS) and checking signature, expiry, and claims.
@HttpExchange (Spring 6) generates HTTP clients from interfaces -- like Feign but Spring-native with no extra dependencies, using RestClient underneath.
WebFlux is the reactive web framework built on Project Reactor: Mono<T> for 0-1 results, Flux<T> for 0-N streamed results, running on a non-blocking event loop.
WebSocket provides full-duplex bidirectional real-time communication (live trading terminal); SSE provides simpler one-way server-to-client streaming (price ticker).
GraphQL lets the client specify exactly which fields to return, eliminating over-fetching and under-fetching problems common with REST.
Spring AI provides a ChatClient abstraction for LLM integration with RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) support.
Quarkus does build-time processing (annotation scanning, proxy generation) for faster startup and lower memory, while Spring Boot does most processing at runtime.

s1_definition.oneliner: OAuth2 Resource Server validates external JWT tokens, @HttpExchange generates declarative REST clients, WebFlux provides reactive Mono/Flux types, WebSocket enables bidirectional real-time communication, and GraphQL lets clients pick exactly the fields they need.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **OAuth2 Resource Server** -- a Spring Security module that validates JWT tokens from an external authorization server (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta) by fetching the issuer's public key and verifying signature, expiry, issuer, and audience claims.
- **@HttpExchange** -- a Spring 6 annotation that generates HTTP client implementations from interfaces, similar to Feign but using Spring's own RestClient; no extra dependencies needed.
- **WebFlux** -- Spring's reactive web framework built on Project Reactor; uses Mono<T> for single-value responses and Flux<T> for streaming multiple values, running on Netty's non-blocking event loop.
- **WebSocket** -- a protocol that provides full-duplex, bidirectional communication over a single TCP connection; ideal for live trading terminals where both client and server push data.
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** -- a simpler one-way streaming protocol where the server pushes events to the client over HTTP; the browser auto-reconnects on disconnection.
- **GraphQL** -- a query language where the client specifies exactly which fields to return in each request, eliminating the over-fetching and under-fetching problems of REST.
s1_definition.analogy: OAuth2 is like showing your Aadhaar card (a JWT issued by the government) at National Bank of India instead of the bank maintaining its own identity system -- the bank just verifies the card is genuine. WebSocket is a live phone call between Rajesh (the trader) and the exchange where both can talk at any time. SSE is the bank texting Priya real-time price updates -- one-way from bank to customer. GraphQL is ordering only the fields you want from the menu instead of getting the entire plate.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  OAuth2 Resource Server Flow
  ═══════════════════════════
  ┌────────────┐    ┌───────────────────┐    ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Client     │    │ Resource Server   │    │ Authorization     │
  │ (Rajesh)   │    │ (Account API)     │    │ Server (Keycloak) │
  └─────┬──────┘    └────────┬──────────┘    └────────┬──────────┘
        │                    │                        │
        │ 1. Login           │                        │
        │───────────────────────────────────────────► │
        │                    │                        │
        │ 2. JWT token       │                        │
        │◄──────────────────────────────────────────  │
        │                    │                        │
        │ 3. GET /api/accounts/SAV2001                │
        │    Authorization: Bearer eyJ...             │
        │───────────────────►│                        │
        │                    │                        │
        │                    │ 4. Fetch JWKS keys     │
        │                    │    (cached after first)│
        │                    │───────────────────────►│
        │                    │◄───────────────────────│
        │                    │                        │
        │                    │ 5. Validate JWT locally│
        │                    │    - signature OK      │
        │                    │    - not expired        │
        │                    │    - issuer matches     │
        │                    │                        │
        │ 6. 200 OK + data   │                        │
        │◄───────────────────│                        │

  Communication Patterns
  ══════════════════════
  REST:      Client ──► Server ──► Client  (request-response)
  SSE:       Client ◄── Server             (one-way stream)
  WebSocket: Client ◄──► Server            (bidirectional)
  GraphQL:   Client ──► Server ──► Client  (client picks fields)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Modern Spring supports multiple communication patterns, each serving a different need. OAuth2 Resource Server validates JWT tokens from an external authorization server like Keycloak, automatically fetching JWKS keys and verifying signature, expiry, and issuer claims. The @HttpExchange annotation in Spring 6 generates declarative HTTP clients from interfaces, replacing Feign with a Spring-native solution backed by RestClient. WebFlux provides reactive Mono and Flux types for non-blocking I/O on Netty's event loop.

At National Bank of India, REST handles account CRUD with OAuth2 JWT security, SSE streams real-time NIFTY50 prices that browsers auto-reconnect to, WebSocket provides bidirectional communication for Rajesh's trading terminal, and GraphQL lets the mobile app request only the balance field while the web app gets the full account details. Each pattern serves a different use case: REST for standard CRUD, SSE for one-way server push, WebSocket for bidirectional real-time, and GraphQL for flexible queries that eliminate over-fetching.

Remember one sentence: OAuth2 Resource Server validates external JWTs, @HttpExchange generates type-safe clients, WebFlux streams with Mono and Flux, and GraphQL lets clients pick exactly the fields they need.
